about.title: How the colony routes
about.intro: AntHocNet is an ant-colony routing protocol for networks with no fixed infrastructure — phones, drones, cars, satellites. This repository implements it once, in a simulator-independent core, and runs that core in ns-3 and in this page.
about.s1: A node with data and no route sends reactive forward ants. Each one that reaches the destination turns into a backward ant.
about.s2: The backward ant walks the path home and leaves pheromone on every hop: more on short, fast paths, less on slow ones.
about.s3: Each data packet picks its next hop at random, weighted by pheromone raised to β = 20 — so the best trail almost always wins.
about.s4: Hellos find neighbours, proactive ants re-sample routes in use, and link-failure notices and repair ants patch a route when a phone walks away.

line.title: Six in a row
line.blurb: Six nodes that each hear only their neighbours, and one flow from end to end. The smallest network where routing is a question at all.
line.honest: Teaching radio: unit disk, 250 m range, 2 Mbit/s, no collisions.

manet.title: Ad hoc MANET (default)
manet.blurb: 30 phones on an open field: the network the AntHocNet papers were written for. Twenty are carried around (random waypoint, 3–15 m/s: walking to cycling) and leave footprints; ten stay put. Links appear and break as people move; the bold trail is each flow's strongest pheromone route, and you can watch it switch.
manet.honest: Teaching radio: unit disk, 250 m range. The measured MANET results use ns-3 two-ray and Nakagami channels.

read.label: Network regimes: the ad hoc field

town.title: Ad hoc town: phones, laptops, PCs
town.blurb: 30 devices in a small town, with no infrastructure: every device is a router. Phones are carried at walking pace and reach 120 m; laptops move now and then and reach 180 m; desktop PCs stay indoors and reach 250 m. A link needs both ends to reach, so a phone next to a PC still only talks across 120 m.
town.honest: Teaching radio: unit disk with a range per device class, 2 Mbit/s. The measured MANET results use one ns-3 radio for every node.

read.label: Network regimes: the ad hoc field

mesh.title: Static Wi-Fi mesh
mesh.blurb: A community mesh: nothing moves. Every link that exists stays. Watch what the ants keep spending once the routes are found.
mesh.honest: Teaching radio: unit disk, 250 m range.

read.label: Network regimes: a mesh that never moves

fanet.title: FANET: a drone swarm
fanet.blurb: 20 drones flying a 3-D Gauss–Markov pattern at about 20 m/s. Links last seconds, not minutes. Altitude is shown as size and shade.
fanet.honest: Teaching radio: 3-D unit disk, 300 m range. The measured FANET results use ns-3 with 3-D Gauss–Markov mobility.

read.label: Network regimes: links that last seconds

vanet.title: VANET: cars in a city
vanet.blurb: 30 vehicles on a Manhattan street grid. Buildings block the radio, so a link dies the moment a car turns a corner.
vanet.honest: Teaching radio: unit disk cut by buildings. The measured VANET results use ns-3 two-ray plus building shadowing.

read.label: Network regimes: links cut by buildings

satellite.title: Satellites: a Walker constellation
satellite.blurb: 64 satellites in 8 orbital planes, 1200 km up at 53°. Satellites in one plane share an orbit (a ring); the planes are turned 45° apart, so each ring is a different orbit. Every satellite keeps four +grid links — ahead and behind in its plane, and to the same slot in the next planes — and their delay changes as the orbits move.
satellite.honest: Teaching orbits: one revolution takes 120 s, about 55× faster than a real 1200 km orbit (109 min), so you can see it move; link delay is the real distance at light speed (≈19 ms in-plane). The measured results use ns-3 LEO mobility (walker16, Starlink shell 1).

missions.title: Missions
missions.campaignNote: The campaign plays these lessons as levels.
missions.total: {n} / {max} stars. Or just play: every tool works outside a mission too.

hello.title: Hello, neighbours
hello.intro: Every node says hello once a second. A node that misses two of a neighbour's hellos in a row forgets that neighbour.
hello.goal: Drag node 5 away from node 4 until node 4 forgets it, then bring it back until they are neighbours again.
hello.debrief: Hellos are how a node learns who it can talk to; the core seeds a small pheromone entry for every new neighbour and drops all of them when the neighbour goes quiet (ADR-0008, detector A).
hints: The radio reaches 250 m: drag node 5 well clear of node 4.
Forgetting takes about two seconds of simulated time; watch the log for "lost neighbour".

run.waiting: Waiting for node 4 to forget node 5…
run.forgot: Node 4 forgot node 5. Now bring node 5 back.
run.done: They met again at t = {t} s: one hello was enough.

scouts.title: Send the scouts
scouts.intro: Node 0 starts sending to node 5 at t = 2 s, but it has never heard of node 5. Before any data moves, it broadcasts a reactive forward ant, which every node rebroadcasts until one reaches node 5.
scouts.goal: Predict how many hops the successful ant travels, then watch it happen.
scouts.debrief: Reactive forward ants flood outward, each remembering the path it took. The first one to arrive turns into a backward ant and walks the same path home.
hints: Each node only hears its immediate neighbours.
Count the gaps between node 0 and node 5.

run.q: How many hops from node 0 to node 5?
run.right: Right. Watch the orange ants fan out.
run.wrong: Let's see: watch the orange ants fan out.
run.done: It took 5 hops. The first packet arrived {ms} ms after it was sent, after {n} reactive ant transmissions.

way-back.title: The way back
way-back.intro: When a forward ant reaches its destination, a backward ant retraces its path. At each hop it deposits pheromone on the link it came from, more for a faster path.
way-back.goal: Node 0 is about to look for node 24. Predict which of its neighbours ends up with the most pheromone toward node 24.
way-back.debrief: The deposit is the inverse of the path's estimated time, averaged into the old value (γ = 0.7). Over time the best link accumulates the most.
hints: Look at where node 24 is on the map.
Fewer hops and less queueing means more pheromone.

run.q: Which neighbour of node 0 will carry the most pheromone toward node 24?
run.picked: You picked node {n}. Watch the blue trail grow from node 0.

scent.title: Follow the scent
scent.intro: A data packet does not follow one fixed route. Each node picks a next hop at random, weighted by pheromone raised to the power β = 20, so the best trail wins most of the time, but not always.
scent.goal: Predict node 0's next hop for eight data packets. You score against the core's own probabilities.
scent.debrief: This is the stochastic routing rule (the paper's Eq. 1). The power β = 20 makes it nearly greedy; a smaller β would spread traffic more evenly across paths.
hints: Use Inspect on node 0: its table shows the exact probability of each choice.
Picking the most likely neighbour every time is the best strategy, but even that can miss.

run.waiting: Waiting for the route to form…
run.q: Packet {r}: where will node 0 send it?
run.went: It went to node {went} (p = {pw}). You picked node {pick} (p = {pp}).
run.done: {hits} of 8 right. Your picks' combined probability was {p} of a possible 8.

two-roads.title: Two roads
two-roads.intro: Because the choice is random, traffic can split over several paths at once. That is multipath routing, and it is AntHocNet's headline feature.
two-roads.goal: Catch any node sending flow 0's packets to two different neighbours.
two-roads.debrief: Multipath spreads load and gives a ready backup when a link breaks. The core only keeps a second path if its ants were nearly as good (the acceptance factor, #96).
hints: Splits happen where two links have similar pheromone.
Drag a node so two paths are equally short.

run.done: Node {n} has sent flow 0 to nodes {a} and {b}: two roads at once.

cut.title: Cut the cable
cut.intro: Links break. The node that notices sends a link-failure notice, and repair ants look for another way while held packets wait.
cut.goal: Bulldoze a node that is carrying flow 0, then see how many packets the network loses in the next 10 s.
cut.debrief: Local repair and multipath keep losses low: often a second trail already exists, and the packets switch to it within a hello period.
hints: Watch for the purple crates of flow 0 and pick a node in the middle of their path.
Fewer losses earn more stars; luck in where you cut matters too.

run.start: Bulldoze a node on flow 0's path.
run.down: Node {n} is down. Counting losses for 10 s…
run.wrong: Node {n} was not carrying flow 0. Bulldoze it again to switch it back on, then pick another.
run.done: Flow 0 lost {n} packet(s); the next delivery came {ms} ms after the cut.
run.doneNever: Flow 0 lost {n} packet(s); the next delivery came never (the flow is cut off).

fresh.title: Keep it fresh
fresh.intro: Proactive ants re-check a route while it is in use, so the trail follows the nodes as they move. This mission turns them off for one run (a labelled mission knob) and compares.
fresh.goal: Watch 40 s with proactive ants off, then 40 s with them on.
fresh.debrief: Proactive sampling costs ants, but on a moving network it finds better routes before the old ones break. On the teaching radio the difference is small and seed-dependent; the measured ablations are on the results pages.
hints: Just watch: the mission runs both halves for you.

run.knob: Mission knob: enableProactive = 0 for this half.
run.done: Off: {offP} delivered, {offA} ant transmissions. On: {onP} delivered, {onA} ant transmissions. Same seed, same movement.

boss.title: Run the city
boss.intro: Three flows cross a moving network that is not always connected. You are the network planner.
boss.goal: From t = 10 s to t = 70 s, deliver at least 95% of all packets. You may place up to 4 relay phones (they stay where you put them).
boss.debrief: Partitions, not routing, cap delivery on sparse mobile networks: no protocol can cross a gap with no radio in it. That is why the measured results include an oracle that knows the whole topology.
hints: Watch where packets are dropped (✕) and place a relay phone to bridge that gap.
A relay in a crowded middle area helps every flow.

run.doneOver: {p} delivered ({d} of {s}) with {n} relay(s) placed — over the limit of 4.

mesh-quiet.title: Mesh: does it ever go quiet?
mesh-quiet.intro: In a static mesh nothing moves and no link ever breaks.
mesh-quiet.goal: Once every route is found, does AntHocNet stop sending ants?
mesh-quiet.debrief: No: proactive ants and hellos keep sampling links that will never change. On the measured static mesh that is why OLSR and DSDV edge out AntHocNet, with lower overhead.
hints: Proactive ants run on a timer while data flows.

run.q: Will the ants stop once the routes are found?
run.done: From t = 20 to 50 s, with every route long established: {n} ant transmissions (not counting hellos).

fanet-relay.title: FANET: faster than the tables
fanet-relay.intro: Drones at 20 m/s keep links for seconds, not minutes.
fanet-relay.goal: Keep delivery at 80% or more from t = 5 to t = 35 s. You may launch up to 2 relay drones.
fanet-relay.debrief: Fast, three-dimensional movement is where AntHocNet measured strongest: its ants re-sample faster than a table protocol's update cycle, and OLSR's delivery collapses.
hints: Launch relays where the swarm thins out between a source and its destination.

vanet-corner.title: VANET: around the corner
vanet-corner.intro: Buildings block the radio. Two cars a block apart can be well within range and still unable to hear each other.
vanet-corner.goal: Wait for a transmission to fail, then say why it failed.
vanet-corner.debrief: On the street grid, links die at corners, not at the edge of radio range. That is why AntHocNet loses so much traffic to reconvergence there (#537), and why its overhead advantage reverses.
hints: Look at whether a building stands between the two cars.

run.q: Node {n} just failed to reach node {p}. Why?
run.building: A building is in the way
run.doneBuilding: They were {d} m apart with a {r} m radio: in range, so a building cut the link.
run.doneFar: They were {d} m apart with a {r} m radio: simply out of range.

sat-failcell.title: Satellites: the failed link
sat-failcell.intro: Inter-satellite links are fixed and predictable, until one fails.
sat-failcell.goal: Cut an inter-satellite link that flow 0 is using, and time how long until its packets get through again.
sat-failcell.debrief: On the measured ISL grid AntHocNet re-converges in about 0.125 s, within 11 ms of an oracle that knows the topology instantly.
hints: Watch flow 0's purple crates, then click the link they ride with Bulldoze.

run.start: Cut a link flow 0 is using.
run.wrong: Flow 0 was not using that link. Try one its packets ride.
run.done: Flow 0 was delivering again {ms} ms after the cut.

phone.label: Phone
phone.note: carried at walking pace; short range

bus.label: Bus
bus.note: a fixed line, the same loop every time

1.title: Ad hoc town
1.blurb: Phones, laptops and PCs talking directly: no routers, no infrastructure. Every device is a router.

2.title: Neighbourhood mesh
2.blurb: Rooftop routers for a village. Nothing moves, so what do the ants keep doing?

3.title: City streets
3.blurb: Cars on a street grid with tall buildings. A link lives only while both ends can see down the same street.

4.title: Forest
4.blurb: Rangers under a forest canopy and relay drones above it. Leaves cut range; batteries run out.

5.title: Orbit
5.blurb: Ground stations and a moving shell of satellites. Links come and go on a schedule set by the orbits.

1_1.title: First hello
1_1.story: Ana and Ben stand on opposite sides of the square, phones in hand. Their phones reach 120 m; they are 220 m apart.
hints: Drag Ben (the phone on the right) towards Ana until the range rings overlap.
Their phones hear each other within 120 m.
1_1.debrief: Once a second each device says hello. A device that hears a hello adds the sender to its neighbour table, with a small pheromone entry for it; two missed hellos and it forgets.

1_2.title: Across the street
1_2.mechanism: reactive forward ants, backward ants and pheromone
1_2.story: Two houses, 340 m apart, want a video call between their desktop PCs, which reach 250 m. You have one laptop to set down in between.
hints: A laptop reaches 180 m, and a link needs both ends to reach.
Put it in the middle of the street, within 180 m of both houses.
1_2.debrief: The first PC had never heard of the second, so it flooded a reactive forward ant. The copy that arrived turned into a backward ant and walked the same path home, laying pheromone on each hop. Data then follows the pheromone.

1_3.title: Follow the scent
1_3.story: A call from the school PC to the library PC can go through either of two laptops. One path has been reinforced by many backward ants; the other only by a few.
hints: Pheromone sets the odds; it does not make the choice alone.
Look at the inspector: each neighbour shows its pheromone and its share of the draws.
1_3.debrief: Data picks a next hop with probability proportional to its pheromone raised to β (20 for data), so a modestly better path takes almost all the traffic while the other stays known. That is how AntHocNet keeps several paths alive at little cost.

quiz1.question: Most of the school's packets go through the laptop with more pheromone. Why "most", and not "all"?
options: Each packet picks a neighbour at random, weighted by pheromone raised to a power β, so the stronger path wins most draws, not every one
Packets alternate between the laptops to share the load
The weaker laptop is only used when the stronger one is busy

1_4.title: The café
1_4.mechanism: proactive ants and the strongest route switching
1_4.story: The café's PC and the bakery's PC talk through whoever is walking by. People wander in and out; when nobody is in the middle, the call drops.
hints: A desktop PC never walks away.
Put it midway between the two shops: 240 m from each.
1_4.debrief: While the call runs, proactive forward ants keep sampling the paths, so when a walker carries a better route past, the strongest route switches to it, and back when they leave. The PC you added is the path that never leaves.

1_5.title: Two ways home
1_5.story: One laptop on a bench carries the whole call between the two houses. At t = 40 s its owner closes the lid.
hints: Before the lid closes, give the call a second way across.
A PC on the other side of the street, within reach of both houses.
1_5.debrief: With a second path, AntHocNet keeps pheromone on both. When the laptop disappears, the houses notice within two missed hellos and the traffic already has somewhere to go; a local repair ant or a link-failure notice fixes what is left.

1_6.title: Rush hour
1_6.mechanism: everything above, and the cost of ants
1_6.story: Three calls cross the town square at rush hour, and a crowd of phones walks through it. You can afford three PCs, but a cheap, quiet network earns more stars.
hints: The three calls all cross the middle of the square.
Every house is within 250 m of the centre: one PC there carries all three calls.
1_6.debrief: Every device you add is another router sending hellos and forwarding ants, so the network's overhead (ants per delivered packet) grows with it. AntHocNet's measured trade on the MANET grid is exactly this: delivery bought with control traffic.

2_1.title: Rooftops
2_1.mechanism: routes found once on a topology that never moves
2_1.story: Four houses want to reach the village gateway in the square. Their home gateways reach 150 m; the square is 400 m away.
hints: A rooftop router reaches 300 m, but a home gateway only 150 m: the router must be near each house.
One router near each house, each within 300 m of the square.
2_1.debrief: On a mesh that never moves, the first backward ants find the routes and they stay found: delivery is near perfect from the first seconds.

2_2.title: Does it ever go quiet?
2_2.mechanism: the cost of proactive sampling on stable links
2_2.story: The village mesh is wired and every route is found. Nothing moves. Watch the ant counter.
hints: Count the ants in the last ten seconds against the first ten.
AntHocNet samples on a timer, not on change.
2_2.debrief: AntHocNet sends hellos every second and proactive ants every ten seconds of a session, however stable the network is. On a static mesh that is pure overhead; a quiet mode that backs off on stable links is planned for v2.3.0 (#571) and will appear here as an upgrade.

quiz1.question: Every route is found and nothing moves. Do the ants stop?
options: No: hellos and proactive ants keep flying at the same rate, whether or not anything changes
Yes: once every route is found, the network goes quiet
Only the hellos stop

2_3.title: Storm
2_3.story: The mesh carries two houses' traffic to the square through one rooftop router. At t = 30 s, lightning takes it down.
hints: The west house only reaches the square through the router at the top-left.
A second router near the west house, on the other side, keeps a path warm.
2_3.debrief: When the router went down, its neighbours missed its hellos and dropped it; the second path you built already had pheromone, so the traffic moved over at once instead of waiting for a new flood.

2_4.title: Wire the village
2_4.story: Six houses, one village gateway, and a budget. Every house must reach the square; the fewer ants it takes, the better.
hints: Each corner house needs a router within 150 m, and that router within 300 m of the square.
The two middle houses are close enough for a repeater each.
2_4.debrief: A mesh is cheapest when each device has just enough neighbours: every extra router adds hellos and ant traffic for every route through it. The measured static-mesh results show AntHocNet delivering almost everything there, and paying for it in control traffic.

3_1.title: Around the corner
3_1.story: Four cars, one call between the two at the ends of a street. Watch what happens to the link when a car turns.
hints: Follow car 1 and watch its links as it reaches a corner.
The radio is the same everywhere. What changes at a corner is what stands between the cars.
3_1.debrief: In a city the distance between two cars is rarely what ends their link: a building does, the moment one of them turns. The measured VANET cell loses about a third of its traffic to exactly this, and a route that was fine a second ago is gone. Link-lifetime prediction (#574) is v2.3.0's attempt to see the break coming.

quiz1.question: The call breaks a moment after a car turns into a side street. Why?
options: The buildings on the corner now block the line of sight between the two cars
The car drove out of radio range
The car's radio switched off at the corner

3_2.title: Roadside units
3_2.mechanism: static relays in a mobile network
3_2.story: Two calls cross the city between cars at its corners. They keep losing each other between blocks. Put roadside units where streets meet.
hints: A unit at a crossing sees down both of its streets.
The inner crossings are the ones most cars pass.
3_2.debrief: A roadside unit never moves, so the links it forms with passing cars last as long as each car stays on one of its two streets. That gives the ants anchors in a network where every other link is short-lived.

3_3.title: Bus line
3_3.mechanism: predictable mobility vs. a fixed relay
3_3.story: Two roadside units at opposite edges of town want to talk. A bus loops the inner ring every couple of minutes. One more unit is all the budget allows.
hints: Does the bus ever see both edge units at once?
The street between the two units crosses the middle of town.
3_3.debrief: The bus is perfectly predictable, but it never stands where it could bridge both units at once, so it never carries the call. A fixed unit in the middle does. Knowing where a link will be is the idea behind the Look-ahead upgrade: link-lifetime prediction, which discounts a next hop whose link is about to break.

3_4.title: Traffic jam
3_4.story: Rush hour: sixteen cars, two calls. At 60 s ten of them park and switch off, and the streets empty. Keep both calls going through both phases.
hints: Dense traffic carries itself; plan for the empty streets.
Corners first, then the centre.
3_4.debrief: When the streets empty, every route the ants built through the parked cars is gone at once, and the network must find new ones. That is reconvergence, the largest single loss measured on the VANET page. Fixed units give the new routes something to stand on.

4_1.title: Under the canopy
4_1.story: Two rangers at either edge of a wood. The trees halve any radio under them. One more ranger radio is all you have.
hints: A radio in the trees reaches half as far.
Look for the clearing.
4_1.debrief: Under the canopy a 300 m radio reaches 150 m. The same distance that works in a clearing fails in the trees. Where a relay stands matters as much as how far apart the ends are.

4_2.title: Eyes in the sky
4_2.story: A valley full of trees: no ground radio crosses it. A relay drone can hover above the canopy, where the leaves do not reach. Its battery is small.
hints: Above 30 m the canopy does not matter.
Watch the drone's battery: what happens after about a minute and a half?
4_2.debrief: Above the trees the drone links both rangers at full range. But a drone is a battery with propellers: when it is empty the link is gone, and the ants must find another way. Swapping drones in time, or routing around tired ones (the Battery saver upgrade, the energy-aware metric), is how FANETs live.

quiz1.question: The drone hovers and the call is perfect. What ends it?
options: The drone's battery runs out and it switches off
The canopy grows
Nothing: a hovering drone links forever

4_3.title: Faster than the tables
4_3.mechanism: why reactive repair beats stale tables at speed
4_3.story: Two drones fly fast patrols between two rangers at opposite corners. The call keeps dropping: the drones move faster than routes settle. You can add hovering relays.
hints: A link to a moving drone lives seconds.
A chain of hovering drones does not move.
4_3.debrief: At UAV speeds a link can end before any table refresh notices. AntHocNet repairs locally and reactively, which helps, but the measured FANET page shows the real lever: more, better-placed relays.

quiz1.question: Why does the call keep dropping while the drones fly fast patrols?
options: Each link lives only seconds, shorter than the time to refresh routes
The drones' batteries are empty
The rangers are too far from each other to ever talk

4_4.title: Lost hiker
4_4.story: A hiker walks a loop on the far side of the wood. Their radio must reach the ranger station at the other edge, across the canopy. Three hovering drones.
hints: The hiker never stops walking: cover the whole loop.
Space the drones so each sees the next.
4_4.debrief: A chain of drones is only as strong as its longest hop, and the hiker moves along one end of it. A swarm that keeps a moving person connected must cover where they may be, not just where they are.

5_1.title: First contact
5_1.story: Paris and Luanda, two ground stations, one call over the shell. Watch the stations' links as the satellites pass.
hints: Select a ground station and watch which satellite it talks to.
Every satellite passes overhead in a minute or two.
5_1.debrief: A ground station sees each satellite for only part of its pass, then hands over to the next. On a real shell that happens every 15 s or so, on a schedule the orbits fix in advance. Every handover is a link break the ants must route around.

quiz1.question: The call keeps working, but the station's link keeps moving to a different satellite. Why?
options: Each satellite sinks below 25° and the station hands over to the next one rising
The satellites are failing one after another
The ground station moves

5_2.title: Across the ocean
5_2.story: New York to Lisbon: no satellite sees both. The call crosses the ocean hop by hop over inter-satellite links.
hints: Count the hops on the route.
Light takes about 3.3 ms per 1000 km.
5_2.debrief: Every inter-satellite hop adds its propagation delay, thousands of kilometres at the speed of light. AntHocNet's default hop time is a Wi-Fi hop's 3 ms; the Long-haul timing upgrade (#205) sets it from the link's real propagation delay.

quiz1.question: What dominates the delay of a packet crossing the ocean over the shell?
options: Propagation: thousands of kilometres per hop at the speed of light
Waiting in queues on the satellites
The ground stations' radios

5_3.title: The failed link
5_3.story: Paris to Luanda over the shell. At 40 s three inter-satellite links fail at once. Predict, then watch.
hints: The +grid has more than one way across.
LinkFail notifications spread the news; the ants find the rest.
5_3.debrief: A +grid shell has many equal paths, so losing a few links costs a reconvergence, not the call. The measured ISL-grid page times exactly this: the detection, then the new route.

quiz1.question: Three links on the route fail at 40 s. What happens to the call?
options: It pauses briefly, then the ants find another way across the grid
It stops for good: those links were the only way
Nothing at all: packets never notice

5_4.title: Solar storm
5_4.story: Two calls cross the shell. At 60 s a solar storm knocks out one satellite in ten. Nothing to build: predict, then watch.
hints: Which routes used a satellite that died?
Repair ants work locally, all at once.
5_4.debrief: A storm breaks many routes at the same moment, and every node near a dead satellite repairs at once. The measured Starlink storm cell shows the dip and the recovery; this level shows the same shape at teaching scale.

quiz1.question: One satellite in ten fails at once. What does the delivery curve do?
options: Dips while routes through the dead satellites are repaired, then recovers
Falls to zero and stays there
Does not change: one in ten is too few to matter

5_5.title: Launch window
5_5.mechanism: why orbits differ: planes and coverage
5_5.story: One orbital plane of the shell is empty: its satellites never launched. Paris and Luanda still talk, but less well. One launch is booked: which plane should it fill?
hints: Look at the gap in the rings of orbits.
Satellites in one plane share one ring.
5_5.debrief: Every plane covers a band of the Earth as it turns. An empty plane is a gap that moves across the map, and the calls that cross it lose their shortest paths. Filling the gap's own plane restores the grid: same-plane and cross-plane links both come back.

quiz1.question: One plane of the shell is empty. Where should the new satellite go?
options: Into the empty plane, so the gap in coverage closes
Into the busiest plane, beside the most satellites
Anywhere: one satellite cannot change coverage

tunnels.title: Tunnels: the ports
tunnels.blurb: Everything the core needs from a simulator, as small interfaces in ports.h: a clock, a random source, timers, the neighbour list, link state and an observer. An adapter implements them; the core never includes a simulator header.

queen.title: Queen chamber
queen.blurb: The protocol: every ant and every data packet goes through AntRouterLogic, which returns a RouteDecision (send, broadcast, drop, deliver) for the adapter to carry out. Pure logic, no I/O.

store.title: Pheromone store
store.blurb: Each node's routing state: regular and virtual pheromone per (neighbour, destination), and the rules that deposit, diffuse and evaporate it.

gate.title: The gate
gate.blurb: What goes on the air: an ant as a plain value type, serialized by the codec into the canonical wire format (wire-format.md).

senses.title: Senses
senses.blurb: How a link is judged: the metric registry and the classic hop + time metric the paper uses.

readme.title: {title} — on ns-3
readme.from: Exported from the AntHocNet learn site (world `{world}`, seed {seed}, {time} s recorded).
readme.intro: The game ran the AntHocNet core on a teaching radio; this kit runs the same scene on ns-3.
readme.step1: An ns-3 tree (3.36–3.48) with AntHocNet in `contrib/`:
readme.step1a: from a checkout: `make install-ns3 NS3DIR=/path/to/ns-3`, or
readme.step1c: or the ready image: `docker run --rm -it -v "$PWD":/kit ghcr.io/danieljoppi/ns3:3.42` (ns-3 in `/opt/ns-3`).
readme.step2: Check it: `make doctor NS3DIR=/path/to/ns-3` (the Workshop's install quest reads its output).
readme.step3: Configure and build ns-3 with examples, then: `NS3DIR=/path/to/ns-3 bash run.sh`.
readme.cmdIntro: The command, if you already have the files:
readme.sat: `run.sh` — the moving Walker shell this world draws (8 planes × 8 satellites, 1200 km, 53°) in `leo-walker`, which needs ns-3 3.48 or later. leo-walker carries its own ground-station flows, so the game's flows are not replayed. With only 64 satellites the stations' elevation mask is lowered to 10° so every city sees one.
readme.mobility: `mobility.ns_movements` — where every node was, as an ns-2 movement trace: its start position, then one `setdest` per 0.5 s leg. 2-D: the game's altitude is dropped.
readme.flows: `flows.txt` — the flows, `src dst start stop cbrBps`, 64-byte packets as `anthocnet-compare` sends them.
readme.run: `run.sh` — `anthocnet-compare` replaying both (`--mobility=trace`, `--flowsFile`), with the channel of this world.
readme.attrs: Your tuning-bench changes, as ns-3 attributes: `{attrs}`.
readme.why: Expect different numbers, and that is the point of running it. The game's radio is a teaching model:
readme.disk: **A unit disk.** Two nodes hear each other perfectly inside the range and not at all outside it. ns-3 here runs Wi-Fi over a range-limited channel (or the urban channel: the same, cut by buildings), with real frame timing.
readme.mac: **No collisions, no MAC contention.** The game delivers every frame on a free link; ns-3's 802.11 MAC contends, backs off, collides and retries, so busy areas lose packets and add delay.
readme.queue: **No queue limits.** ns-3's interface queues fill and drop.
readme.core: **The same core.** Every routing decision in both is the AntHocNet core's; only the radio and the MAC below it differ.
readme.published: This is a built-in world at its default seed. The measured, multi-seed ns-3 results for its network family are on [{label}]({href}).
